claims.text: The marketing mix is the combination of decisions a business makes about its product, its price, its promotion and the place it is sold through, planned together so that the product reaches its chosen market in a form, at a price, with a message and through an outlet that market accepts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Product covers what is sold, including its design, features, quality, range, packaging and the service around it. Price covers the amount charged and the method used to arrive at it. Promotion covers how the business communicates with the market. Place covers the route the product takes to reach the buyer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The four elements are decided together because each of them signals something to the buyer, so a mix whose parts point in different directions - a premium product sold cheaply through a discount outlet - weakens the position the business is trying to hold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The weight given to each element varies with the product and the market. A differentiated consumer good in a crowded market usually leans on promotion and branding, while a standard input sold to industrial buyers often turns mainly on price, reliability and delivery.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The mix serves a marketing objective and a chosen target segment, so a decision to aim at a different segment usually forces changes in more than one element rather than in one alone.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The 4Ps are not a checklist to be worked through in order. They are four decisions that constrain one another, so changing any one of them may require the other three to be revisited.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Goods are physical items that can be made in advance, stored, owned and resold. Services are acts performed for a customer, produced at the moment they are used.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Four working differences follow from that. A service is intangible, so a buyer cannot inspect it before buying. It is perishable, so capacity not used at the time cannot be kept for later. It is inseparable from the person or system delivering it, so the delivery is part of what is bought. And it is harder to repeat identically, so consistency has to be managed rather than assumed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because a service cannot be inspected before purchase, buyers rely on substitutes for inspection - price, premises, reputation, the appearance and manner of staff, reviews and guarantees - which is why a service business puts weight on those signals in its marketing mix.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Most offerings combine the two. A restaurant sells food, which is a good, and the cooking and serving of it, which is a service; a vehicle dealership sells a bakkie alongside a warranty and a servicing plan.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The tangible attributes of a product are the features that can be seen, touched or measured: size, materials, performance, durability and the packaging it comes in.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The intangible attributes of a product are the features a buyer cannot physically examine: brand reputation, the status attached to owning it, after-sales support, a guarantee, and the convenience of buying it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Buyers may pay more for intangible attributes than the physical product alone would earn, and those attributes are usually slower for a rival to copy than a physical feature, which is why a business invests in reputation and service as well as in the product itself. The premium holds while the tangible performance keeps supporting the reputation; where the product stops delivering, the intangible attribute decays with it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A product is bought as a bundle of both kinds of attribute, so a decision about one - cheaper materials, a shorter guarantee - changes the value of the bundle even when the other side of it is untouched.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Product development is the work of improving an existing product or creating a new one for the business to sell.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Products lose appeal as tastes, technology and competitors move, so a business that does not develop its products is likely to find revenue falling as its existing products age, with nothing prepared to replace them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Development can open a new segment, support a higher price, make use of spare capacity and reduce the business's dependence on a single product.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Development spending is committed before any revenue arrives from it, and some projects do not reach the market at all, so development has to be financed out of the earnings of existing products or from external finance, and the risk of the spending is carried by the business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Product differentiation is making a product distinguishable from competing products in ways buyers notice and value, through features, quality, design, service, branding or packaging.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A unique selling point is the single feature or benefit a product has that competing products do not, used as the centre of the message the business puts to the market.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Differentiation is the general activity of making a product distinguishable; a unique selling point is one claimable point of difference singled out of it. A product can be differentiated in several small ways without having a unique selling point at all.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where differentiation succeeds, the nearest alternative is no longer an equal substitute, so a price rise costs the business less volume than it would for an undifferentiated product and a premium can be held. That holds while buyers value the difference and while rivals have not matched it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Differentiation may be real, where the product genuinely differs, or perceived, where the difference is created by branding and promotion. Both can support a premium, but a perceived difference is easier for a rival to attack, because the product underneath it is the same.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The product life cycle describes the pattern of sales a product is expected to follow over its life, usually set out in five stages: development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: In development there are no sales and spending only. At introduction sales are low, promotion is heavy and cost per unit is high, so a loss is common. In growth sales rise quickly, unit costs fall, distribution widens and competitors enter. In maturity sales growth flattens, the market is close to saturated and competition turns to price, and this is usually where profit is highest. In decline sales fall and the business decides whether to support the product, take what cash it still yields, or withdraw it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each stage changes the marketing mix. Promotion moves from informing to persuading and then to reminding, price comes under pressure as rivals arrive, distribution widens through growth, and the product itself is varied to hold interest once the market matures.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An extension strategy is an action taken to lengthen the maturity stage of a product and postpone its decline.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Extension strategies include new variants, sizes or flavours, new uses for the product, new segments or export markets, restyling and repackaging, price reductions, a fresh promotion campaign, and selling through a channel the product has not used before.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An extension strategy is worth undertaking where the additional contribution it earns exceeds what it costs and the change still fits the position the product holds. Where sales are falling because the product has been technically replaced, extension usually postpones decline rather than reversing it, and the same money may do more in a replacement product.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The life cycle describes a common pattern rather than a law. The length and shape of the curve differ between products and cannot be read off in advance, falling sales may be a marketing failure rather than maturity, and a business that labels a product as declining and withdraws support from it can bring about the fall it predicted.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The Boston Matrix classifies the products in a business's portfolio on two measures: the share of the market the product holds relative to its largest competitor, and the rate at which that market is growing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The matrix gives four positions. A star holds a high relative share in a fast-growing market, earns a great deal and spends a great deal defending its share. A cash cow holds a high relative share in a slow-growing market and generates more cash than it needs. A question mark holds a low relative share in a fast-growing market and absorbs cash while its future is undecided. A dog holds a low relative share in a slow-growing market and neither earns nor absorbs much.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The matrix is used to judge whether a portfolio is balanced, to decide where the cash generated by cash cows is directed, to show how far the business depends on a small number of products, and to inform decisions about which products to support and which to withdraw.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The matrix rests on two measures and leaves others out, so it informs a decision rather than settling one. Relative market share is not the same as profitability, the answer changes with how widely the market is defined, and a product in a weak position may still earn its place where it completes a range buyers expect or uses capacity that has no better use.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A position in the matrix is a snapshot. Products move between positions as their markets grow or slow and as their share changes, so the matrix is most useful when the same products are plotted repeatedly and the direction of travel is read alongside the current position.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Product portfolio analysis is the practice of examining all the products a business sells together, rather than judging each one on its own.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Looking at the portfolio as a whole changes how a marketing budget is allocated, because spending can be directed to the products where it changes the outcome instead of being spread evenly across the range.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Portfolio analysis shows whether there are products coming through to replace those approaching decline, so a business can start development before the gap in revenue opens rather than after it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Portfolio analysis makes dependence visible: where a large share of revenue comes from one product or one market, the business can see the exposure and decide whether to widen the range.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The position a product occupies shapes its own mix. A product with a high share of a slow-growing market is usually supported with reminder advertising and wide availability, while a new product in a fast-growing market usually needs promotion that generates trial and a price set to win share.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The conclusions depend on the data behind them and on where the boundary of the market is drawn, so a product's portfolio position is evidence to be weighed alongside cost, capacity and strategy rather than an instruction to act.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A pricing method is the rule a business uses to arrive at the price it charges for a product.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A price sits between two limits. Over time the revenue from a product has to cover the costs of supplying it, which sets a floor, and no more can be charged than buyers are prepared to pay given the alternatives open to them, which sets a ceiling. The method chooses a point between the two.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A pricing method is chosen to serve an objective: entering a market and winning share, recovering development spending quickly, defending share against a rival, filling capacity that would otherwise be unused, signalling quality, or simply covering cost with a margin.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: How useful a method is depends on how sensitive demand is to price, how differentiated the product is, how many competitors there are and how quickly they can respond, the stage the product has reached in its life cycle, whether the business can separate groups of buyers or change its prices quickly, and what its costs are.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses commonly use more than one method at once and change method over a product's life: a launch price set to win share, a cost figure acting as a floor beneath it, and a price that follows competitors once the market has settled.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Competitive pricing sets the price of a product by reference to what competitors charge - at, just below, or just above the going rate.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where products are similar and buyers compare prices easily, a price well above the going rate loses volume quickly, so the price is set largely by the market rather than by the business, and competitive pricing accepts that rather than fighting it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Competitive pricing helps a business avoid losing volume to a rival on price and avoid starting a price war by accident. It also needs little information, which suits a small business that cannot research what buyers would pay.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Its weakness is that it looks outward and not inward. Matching a larger rival's price may mean matching a cost base the business does not have, so the margin left may be too thin to cover its own overheads; and a genuinely differentiated product priced at the going rate gives up the premium its difference could earn.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Penetration pricing sets a low price when a product is launched, in order to build sales volume and market share quickly, with the intention of raising the price once the product is established.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A low launch price lowers the cost to a buyer of trying something unfamiliar, so trial rises; rising volume gets the product into more outlets and lowers cost per unit as output grows, which in turn makes the low price easier to sustain. The chain holds where demand is sensitive to price and the business can supply the volume; where either of those fails, the low price buys little extra volume and costs margin on every unit sold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Penetration pricing suits a market where buyers compare on price, where the product is not strongly differentiated, and where the business has the finance to accept a thin margin while volume builds.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The method carries three risks. The thin margin has to be financed until volume arrives. Raising the price later may lose the buyers the low price attracted. And a low launch price can fix the product in buyers' minds as a cheap one, which limits what it can charge afterwards.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Price skimming sets a high price when a product is launched, aimed at the buyers least sensitive to price, and lowers it in stages as that group is served and competitors appear.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A high launch price earns a large margin on each early sale, so development spending is recovered sooner, and the price itself signals that the product is new and distinctive. As the buyers willing to pay most are served, each reduction opens the product to a further group, so the same product is sold at several prices over its life.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Skimming depends on the product being genuinely new or distinctive, on there being a group of buyers who value having it early, and on something that delays imitation, such as a patent, scarce know-how or a lead in distribution.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Its risks run the other way from penetration. The high price limits early volume, so cost per unit stays high; a visibly large margin attracts competitors into the market; and buyers who paid the launch price may resent a later cut, which damages the relationship the brand depends on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Price discrimination is charging different prices to different groups of buyers for the same or a very similar product, where the difference in price is not explained by a difference in the cost of supplying them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: It requires three conditions: the business can identify and separate the groups, the groups differ in how sensitive they are to price, and buyers in the cheaper group cannot easily resell to the dearer one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Charging each group a price closer to what it is prepared to pay raises total revenue above what a single price earns, because the business keeps the high price from buyers who would pay it while still making sales to buyers who would not.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Common bases for separating groups are the time of use, such as off-peak fares; the identity of the buyer, such as student or pensioner rates; and location, such as separate resident and international rates at a lodge.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Discrimination can be resented where the basis for the difference looks unfair, and where a price difference rests on a characteristic that national law protects it may be unlawful. The precise rules depend on the jurisdiction, so a business checks the law of the country it trades in before setting prices this way.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Dynamic pricing changes the price of a product frequently in response to current demand, remaining capacity, the time of purchase or competitors' prices, usually through software that resets the price automatically.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: It suits businesses whose prices can be changed cheaply and quickly, which in practice usually means selling online, and whose capacity is fixed and perishable, such as airline seats, hotel rooms, lodge beds and event tickets.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: When demand is weak the price falls far enough to sell capacity that would otherwise earn nothing, and when demand is strong the price rises to capture what buyers are prepared to pay, so the revenue earned from a fixed capacity rises relative to a single posted price. The gain depends on demand genuinely varying in a way the business can observe, and on buyers not simply postponing the purchase until the price falls.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The costs are the systems and data it needs, the risk that buyers treat frequent changes as unfair or stop trusting the posted price, and the speed with which competitors can see an online price and match it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Dynamic pricing and price discrimination overlap but are not the same. Dynamic pricing varies the price with when a purchase is made and with the state of demand at that moment; price discrimination varies it with which group the buyer belongs to.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost-based pricing sets the price from the business's own cost figure plus an addition, most commonly as cost-plus pricing, where price per unit = cost per unit + (cost per unit x mark-up percentage).

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A mark-up is expressed as a percentage of cost; a margin is the same money expressed as a percentage of the price. A product costing N$40 sold with a 25% mark-up is priced at N$50, and the N$10 of profit in that price is a 20% margin.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The cost figure used may be full cost per unit, which covers the whole of the business's spending at an assumed level of output, or variable cost, which is used as a floor when quoting for a one-off order. Full costing and contribution costing are set out in topic 5.4.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost-based pricing is simple, needs no market research, and gives every sale a margin over the cost figure used. Its weaknesses are that cost per unit depends on an assumed output, so selling fewer units than assumed leaves part of the fixed costs uncovered, and that the calculation never looks outside the business at what buyers would pay or what rivals charge.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Psychological pricing sets a price at a level chosen for how buyers read it rather than for what the arithmetic requires.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: It takes two common forms. Pricing just below a round figure, such as N$99.95 rather than N$100, so the price is read as belonging to a lower band. And pricing deliberately high, so that the price itself is taken as a signal of quality where the buyer has no other way of judging it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Psychological pricing differs from competitive and cost-based pricing in what it takes as its reference point. Competitive pricing looks at the rival's price, cost-based pricing at the business's own cost, and psychological pricing at how the buyer interprets the number itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The money involved is small - five cents below N$100 - but it applies to every unit sold and costs nothing to adopt. Its limits are that experienced buyers may see through it, that a price ending in .95 signals a value position which does not suit every product, and that a high price signals quality for only as long as the product supports the claim.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Promotion is the part of the marketing mix that communicates with the market: telling people the product exists, persuading them to buy it, and reminding those who already buy it. In topic 2.2 the same word means moving an employee to a higher position, which is a different idea altogether.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The objectives of a promotion campaign may be to create awareness at launch, to inform buyers about what the product does and where to get it, to persuade buyers to choose it rather than a rival, to remind existing buyers and defend share in maturity, to support the price position the business wants to hold, or to shift a stated quantity within a stated period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Above-the-line promotion is paid communication placed in media the business does not control, such as television, radio, press, outdoor sites and paid online advertising. Below-the-line promotion is communication the business controls directly, such as sales promotions, direct mail, personal selling, sponsorship and point-of-sale display.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which method is useful depends on what the campaign is for, what the budget is, who the audience is and which media reach it, whether the product is an everyday consumer good or a technical product sold to a few buyers, and whether the result can be measured well enough to judge the spending afterwards.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Methods are normally combined into a promotional mix, because they do different jobs: advertising builds recognition over months while a sales promotion moves stock this week.

claims.text: Advertising is paid communication of a message about a product through a medium, addressed to many people at once, with the business controlling what the message says.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Informative advertising sets out facts a buyer needs - what the product does, what it costs, where to get it. Persuasive advertising works on preference and image rather than on information. Most campaigns carry some of both.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Advertising reaches a large number of people for a low cost for each person reached, and repetition builds recognition that makes later messages cheaper to land. The low cost for each person reached holds where the audience the medium delivers matches the target market; a national campaign for a product sold in one town pays for reach it cannot use.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Advertising is paid for before the result is known, its effect builds slowly and is hard to separate from other causes such as a price change or a rival's difficulties, and the sums involved put the main media out of reach for a small business. That is why a business measures what it can - recall, enquiries, sales in the advertised area - rather than assuming the spending worked.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Sales promotion is a short-term incentive attached to a product to encourage an immediate purchase: a discount, a buy-one-get-one offer, a coupon, a free sample, loyalty points, a competition or a point-of-sale display.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An incentive lowers the cost, or raises the value, of buying now, so some buyers bring a purchase forward and some switch from a rival for the period of the offer. Sales measured during the offer therefore overstate what it has won, because part of the increase is buying that would have happened later anyway.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Sales promotion suits a defined short-term objective: getting trial of a new product, clearing stock before it dates, meeting a target within a quarter, or answering a rival's offer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Its limitations follow from the same mechanism. The effect largely stops when the offer stops; the discount is given on units that would have sold at full price as well as on the extra ones; and repeated offers teach buyers to wait for the next one, which lowers the price the product can hold between offers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Direct promotion is communication addressed to identified individuals rather than to an audience in general, and asking for a response: addressed mail, email, text messages, telephone calls, catalogues and personal selling.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because each message goes to a named person whose response can be traced, the business can measure the response rate and the cost of each sale won, which makes direct promotion easier to judge than advertising and easier to improve by testing one version against another.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Direct promotion suits a high-value product, or a market where the buyers are few and identifiable, which is why it is used heavily where one business sells to another. It depends on a list of contacts that is accurate and permitted to be used.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Its cost for each person contacted is high beside advertising, poor data wastes the spending, and unsolicited contact may be treated as intrusive and damage the brand. Rules on holding personal data and on contacting people without their consent differ between countries, so a business checks what applies where it trades.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Digital promotion is promotion carried through internet-connected channels: the business's own website, search advertising and search optimisation, social media, video platforms, email, mobile apps and messaging, and arrangements with influencers and affiliates.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Four developments separate it from earlier media. Messages can be targeted by interest, location and past behaviour rather than bought by audience in bulk. Responses are counted, so spending can be tied to clicks and to sales. Communication runs both ways, so buyers publish their own view of the product where other buyers see it. And the entry cost is low enough that a small business can reach a national audience without a media budget.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where most people reach the internet on a mobile phone, as they do across much of southern Africa, a campaign designed for a desktop screen reaches the device but not the reader, so digital promotion is built mobile-first and kept light enough to load on a slow connection.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The limits are real. Platform rules and ranking systems change without notice, and reach that was free can disappear. Negative comment spreads as fast as the message. A click counted is not a sale made. And the channel misses buyers who are not online, which in Namibia varies sharply between urban and rural areas and with the cost of mobile data.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Packaging is the material a product is contained in. It protects the product, holds a convenient quantity, identifies it, and carries the information the buyer and the law require.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The promotional work of packaging is done at the point of sale. On a shelf of alternatives the pack is the last message a buyer sees before choosing, so its colour, shape and name act as a silent advertisement and connect the product to whatever the buyer already knows of the brand.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Packaging also differentiates and positions. A resealable pack, a portion size that suits a single household, or a heavier material that feels expensive each change what the product is worth to a buyer without changing what is inside it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Elaborate packaging adds cost to every unit and adds waste, and buyers and regulators in many countries now weigh that, so a business balances the promotional gain against the cost per unit and the reaction to the waste it creates.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A brand is the name, symbol, design and reputation that identify a product as one business's and separate it from competing products.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A recognised brand makes every other piece of promotion work harder, because the message starts from something the buyer already knows rather than from nothing, and it lowers the risk the buyer feels in choosing, because the brand carries a promise that this purchase will be like the last one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Branding supports a price premium, makes retailers more willing to stock the product because customers ask for it by name, and lowers the cost of launching a related product under the same name.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A brand is built slowly and can be damaged quickly by a failure of quality or conduct, because what is broken is the promise the brand carries. It attracts imitation, and its value rests on the product continuing to deliver what the brand claims; where it stops doing so, the brand speeds up the loss of custom rather than slowing it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A channel of distribution is the route a product takes from the producer to the final consumer, together with the businesses that handle it on the way.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Four channel shapes are commonly described: producer direct to consumer; producer to retailer to consumer; producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer; and producer to an agent or distributor and then onward through wholesaler and retailer, which is the usual route into an export market.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An intermediary holds stock, breaks bulk, reaches outlets the producer could not serve and often extends credit, so it widens the reach of the product. Each intermediary takes a margin, so the producer's revenue for each unit falls as the channel lengthens, and the producer loses some control over the price and presentation the buyer sees.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Channel choice serves objectives: making the product available where the target market shops, controlling how it is priced and presented, keeping down the cost of each unit delivered, getting the product to the buyer quickly, covering enough of the market, and receiving feedback from the people who sell it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Distribution intensity is a separate decision. Intensive distribution places the product in as many outlets as possible and suits everyday goods bought on impulse. Selective distribution uses a limited number of outlets chosen for their fit with the product. Exclusive distribution appoints a single outlet or distributor for an area, which protects the brand's position and the dealer's margin at the cost of availability.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which channel suits a business turns on the value and perishability of the product, how technical it is and how much explanation it needs, how widely its customers are spread, and how much finance and control the producer has. A producer in Windhoek selling to shops in Oshakati, Katima Mulilo and Luderitz may find a wholesaler covers ground it could not cover itself, and pays a margin for that reach.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Physical distribution moves the product to the buyer as a physical item, through transport, warehousing, stockholding and shops. Digital distribution delivers the product itself electronically over a network.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Selling online is not the same as distributing digitally. An order placed and paid for on a website for goods that are then driven to the buyer is physical distribution with a digital sales channel; digital distribution means the thing bought - software, a recording, an e-book, an insurance policy, a course - travels as data.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For a product that genuinely travels as data, the cost of supplying one more copy is close to nothing, the seller cannot run out of stock, and distance adds almost no cost, so a small business can serve a national or foreign market from one location.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Digital distribution needs connectivity and a payment method the buyer holds, and the product is easy to copy without paying for it. Physical distribution reaches buyers who are not online and lets the buyer inspect the goods, but its cost rises with distance and the stock it requires ties up cash. Most businesses use both, and in a country with long distances between towns the cost of the final stage of the physical journey is often what decides whether an online order is worth fulfilling.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
